new_statements.quote: Caddo is a tone language in the sense that the low or high tone of many syllables is lexically determined. For example, the word kúkahyánda'ah 'not finding it' in (5) begins with the high tone negative prefix kú-, which is followed by the low tone subordinating prefix kak- (whose syllable-final k became h). However, other instances of high tone syllables are the result of reconstructible changes, as when the high tone in the third syllable of this same word was compensatory for the loss of an i following the n; thus *kúkakyanidaʔak became ...
new_statements.citation: Chafe, Wallace. 2005. Caddo. In Heather K. Hardy & Janine Scancarelli (eds.), Native Languages of the Southeastern United States, 323-350. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press.
new_statements.locator: p. 331 (Google Books search-within hit page_id PA331; text stitched from three overlapping snippets of the same passage)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Caddo is described as a tone (pitch) language, not a stress language: every syllable nucleus carries low (unmarked), high (acute) or falling (grave; always long) tone. Tone is partly lexical (e.g. negative prefix kú- high, subordinator kak- low; past tense marker hít# high) and partly derived by regular processes (h before CC deleted with compensatory high tone; low-tone vowel deleted after a sonorant with high tone on the preceding vowel; high tone spreads leftward across a sonorant; in prepenultimate syllables of a phrase glottal stop is replaced by length and high pitch becomes falling in fast speech). No positional word-stress rule is given, and none of the modern descriptions (Chafe 1976, 2005, 2017; Melnar 2004) mentions stress in any snippet retrieved; Melnar 2004 has zero hits for the word 'stress' in Google's full-text index. Chafe 2017 p.601 confirms: vowels have 'low pitch (unmarked) or high pitch (á, á:). Long vowels may also have falling pitch (à:).'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone is not fully lexical: many high tones are compensatory (lost vowel or deleted h), and fast-speech rules apply to any prepenultimate syllable of a phrase rather than of a word (Chafe 1976). The 1963 IJAL summary of Da Cruz's unpublished analysis claimed 'length, stress, and pitch are phonemic' in Caddo — an older analysis Chafe did not adopt.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical/morphological tone; Chafe 1976 notes some pitch rules (high > falling, ʔ > length) operate over the phrase in fast speech.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern descriptions (Chafe 1976/2005/2017/2018, Melnar 2004) describe the single surviving Oklahoma variety recorded from speakers in Caddo County, OK (Chafe's fieldwork 1960-70); historical dialects (Kadohadacho, Hasinai, Natchitoches, etc.) have no separate Glottolog codes and are not distinguished in the tone statements. The 1963 IJAL/Da Cruz note ('length, stress, and pitch are phonemic') is an earlier, unpublished analysis of the same variety that Chafe's work superseded.

sources.note: Source of the quoted statement; the full phonology section (pp. ~324-333) is needed to confirm the page context, the tone inventory paragraph before p.331, and to verify there is no separate stress remark.

'Caddo has three lexical tones: a low tone... a high tone... and falling tone, which always occurs on long vowels'; tone is lexical, derived by tonological processes (h-deletion, low-tone deletion, backwards assimilation) and morphological (past tense = high tone). No stress mentioned. Tertiary.
